summary: This is a humorous April 1st memo that defines a MIME content type for transporting matter, specifically a sentient life form, across the network. It is a joke and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an April 1st joke about sending a person as email content. It describes the imaginary format in serious technical language, then lists absurd implementation problems.

subtitle: An April 1st joke that proposes a MIME type for transporting sentient life forms.

tldr.problem: The memo's comic premise is that MIME should support sending an entire sentient life form as message content.
tldr.mechanism: It describes a fictional matter-transport/sentient-life-form type with dimensions, scan resolution, and a stream of molecular descriptions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1437 is an April 1st joke document, not a real transport protocol. Its implementation and gateway warnings continue the parody.

sections.title: The Fictional MIME Type
sections.content:
This memo is an April 1st joke. It proposes a new MIME type, matter-transport/sentient-life-form, for messages containing an entire sentient being, such as a human.

The stated design goals include simple parsing, robust reconstruction through gateways, extensibility for other species, and compatibility with SGML. These claims are part of the document's parody of technical specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC pretends that email could carry a person by describing the body as machine-readable matter. The premise is intentionally comic.

sections.title: Dimensions and Molecular Data
sections.content:
The fictional content-type parameters give height, width, and depth in centimeters and scan resolution in Angstroms. The stream is described as a sequence of molecular formulas for locations in the three-dimensional solid, with spaces separating formulas.

The example uses an intentionally simplified depiction of a politician. The memo says quoted-printable may be needed to prevent line wrapping from disrupting very long molecular descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The imagined message gives the size and detail of a three-dimensional scan, then lists molecules at each location. The sample data and claims are part of the joke.

sections.title: Gateway and Storage Warnings
sections.content:
The memo jokes about gateways rejecting life-bearing messages, file-system space errors truncating a laboratory rat, byte-order problems, and a person arriving upside down. It also warns about duplicate delivery producing duplicate people.

Its security section speculates about using the fictional mechanism to evade extradition or delay legal proceedings. The absurd warnings reinforce that this is satire rather than a deployable MIME extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors imagine data corruption, duplicate delivery, and bad gateways producing bizarre outcomes. These warnings are part of the April 1st humor.
